ox: Correct. p53 is a tumor suppressor. After DNA damage it stops the cell at the G1/S checkpoint so repair can happen. If damage is too bad, it triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death).
Wrong. Oncogenes push the cell to divide. p53 does the opposite. Trap: confusing tumor suppressors with oncogenes.
Wrong. Cyclins rise and fall with the cell cycle. p53 is a transcription factor that turns genes on or off, not a cyclin.
Wrong. Telomerase lengthens telomeres (chromosome ends). It is not related to p53's role.

concept.t: p53, the guardian of the genome
p: p53 is a protein that checks for DNA damage. It is a tumor suppressor: a gene whose job is to stop uncontrolled growth.
When DNA is damaged, p53 turns on genes (like p21) that pause the cycle at G1/S. If repair fails, p53 pushes the cell into apoptosis.

mem: p53 = tumor suppressor; loss of p53 helps cancer grow.
It arrests the cell at G1/S or triggers apoptosis.
Oncogenes speed division; tumor suppressors brake it.
q26.trap: Calling p53 an oncogene. Loss of a tumor suppressor causes cancer; gain of an oncogene does.
q26.plain: p53 is a safety inspector who stops the factory line when something is broken, and shuts down the machine if it cannot be fixed.

ox: Correct. Ectoderm is the outer germ layer. It forms the epidermis (skin) and the nervous system.
Wrong. Heart and kidneys come from mesoderm, the middle layer. Trap: thinking of organs in general as outer structures.
Wrong. Gut lining and lungs come from endoderm, the inner layer.
Wrong. Bone and skeletal muscle come from mesoderm.

p: Early embryos have three layers of cells. Each becomes different body parts.
Ectoderm (outer): skin and nervous system. Mesoderm (middle): muscle, bone, heart, kidneys, blood. Endoderm (inner): gut lining, lungs, liver, pancreas.

mem: Ectoderm = skin (epidermis) + nervous system.
Mesoderm = muscle, bone, heart, kidney, blood.
Endoderm = gut lining, lungs, liver, pancreas.
q27.trap: Mixing up mesoderm and endoderm for organs such as kidneys and lungs.
q27.sc: Ecto = outer, like exterior: the outer layer makes the outer covering (skin) and the nervous system. Endo = inner, like the gut lining.
q27.plain: Think of a three-layer cake. The top layer becomes the skin and the brain, the middle becomes muscles and bones, the bottom becomes the insides of tubes like the gut.

ox: Wrong. In prophase, chromatin condenses into chromosomes and the spindle begins to form. The chromatids are still joined.
Wrong. In metaphase, chromosomes line up at the middle plate. They are still paired. Trap: this is just before the separation.
Correct. In anaphase, cohesin (the protein glue holding sister chromatids) is cleaved. The chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.
Wrong. In telophase, nuclear envelopes re-form around the separated sets. Separation already happened.

p: A sister chromatid is one of two identical copies of a chromosome, joined at the centromere. Mitosis splits them so each new cell gets one copy.
The order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Splitting happens in anaphase.

mem: Prophase: condense. Metaphase: line up. Anaphase: apart. Telophase: two nuclei.
Anaphase = sister chromatids separate (mitosis).
In meiosis I, homologs separate; in meiosis II, sister chromatids separate.
q28.mn: PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase. 'A' for Apart.
q28.trap: Picking metaphase because it is the famous lineup stage. Separation comes right after it.
q28.plain: Two kids holding hands line up in the middle of the room (metaphase). In anaphase someone lets go and each kid walks to opposite sides.

ox: Wrong. 70% is the viability at 30 µM, the lowest point of the curve. The question asks about 60 µM.
Wrong. 85% is the viability at 10 µM. Picking it means you read the wrong row.
Correct. Table 1 lists the 60 µM row with a 24 h time and a viability of 95%.
Wrong. 110% is the viability at 100 µM, the highest value. It is the next row down from 60 µM.

concept.t: Reading a value from a table
p: A table is a grid. Each row is one group. To answer, find the row that matches the question (here 60 µM), then read across to the column you need (Viability %).
A µM (micromolar) is a unit of concentration, meaning how much compound is dissolved in the liquid.

bp1000_0.plain: It is like finding a friend's name in a class list and reading the grade next to it. Make sure you are on the right line.
mem: Find the row first, then the column.
Check the units and the column header before choosing.
Neighbouring rows are the usual wrong answers.
bp1000_0.trap: The distractors are the other rows of the same table (70, 85, 110). Reading the wrong row is the whole trap.

ox: Wrong. The 0 µM vehicle control gives the baseline (100%) to compare against, but it does not show the shape of the curve. Two points could never show a fall and then a rise.
Wrong. A single time point (24 h) tells you nothing about the shape across concentrations. Shape depends on how many concentrations you test, not how many times you measure.

Correct. The passage describes five groups: 0, 10, 30, 60 and 100 µM. With several concentrations the data show 100, 85, 70, 95, 110, a fall then a rise (U-shape). Fewer points could look like a straight line.
Wrong. The MTT assay at 570 nm is the way viability is measured. It affects accuracy, not whether you can see a U-shape.

concept.t: Why many doses reveal a curve
p: A dose-response design tests several amounts of a treatment. Each amount gives one dot on a graph. The more dots, the better you can see the true shape.
With only two or three dots, any curve looks like a straight line. A bend only shows up when you have a dot on each side of it.

bp1000_1.plain: If you only check a hill at the bottom and the top, you think it is a straight ramp. You need stops along the way to see the bump.
mem: More dose levels means better shape detection.
Control = baseline, not shape.
Assay choice affects measurement quality, not curve shape.
bp1000_1.trap: Choosing the control or the assay because they sound like good design. The question asks about shape, which depends on number of dose levels.

ox: Wrong. 10 is the raw difference in percentage points (95 - 85). Percent change must be divided by the starting value 85, so it is not 10%.
Correct. Percent change = (new - old) / old x 100. Table 1 gives 85% at 10 µM and 95% at 60 µM. The change is 10, and 10/85 is about 0.12, so about 12% increase.
Wrong. 15% would need a change of about 13 points (15% of 85). The actual change is only 95 - 85 = 10.
Wrong. 25% would need a change of about 21 points. It is far too large for a 10-point rise.

p: Percent change tells you how big a change is compared with where you started. You divide the change by the starting value, then turn it into a percent.
Do not confuse percentage points (the plain subtraction of two percentages) with percent change (relative to the start).

bp1000_2.plain: If your pizza goes from 85 slices-worth to 95, you gained 10, but 10 compared to 85 is a bit over one-tenth.
mem: Percent change = (new - old) / old x 100.
Always divide by the starting value.
Points difference is not percent change.

fm.f: Percent change = (new value - old value) / old value x 100, where old value = viability at 10 µM and new value = viability at 60 µM
fm.why: The question asks for change from one group to another, relative to the first group.
fm.nc: 10/85 is close to 10/80 = 1/8 = 12.5%, so the answer is just under 12.5%, matching 12%.

bp1000_2.sc: Estimate: 10 over a bit more than 80 is slightly under 1/8, about 12%. Only one option is near that.
bp1000_2.trap: Answering 10% because the raw difference is 10. The denominator 85 makes it a little higher.

ox: Correct. This is the NOT supported statement. The word 'always' is too strong. Table 1 shows viability falls from 100 at 0 µM to 85 at 10 µM and 70 at 30 µM, so higher concentration did not always raise viability. Only from 30 µM upward did it rise.
Wrong. This is supported. The passage says the lowest viability was at 30 µM, and the table shows 70%, lower than every other group.
Wrong. This is supported. The passage states n = 6 per group.
Wrong. This is supported. The passage says the researchers performed an ANOVA to determine significance between groups.

p: In a NOT question, three options are true and one is false or unsupported. Check each option against the passage and pick the one that fails.
Words like always, never, only and all are red flags. One counterexample in the data makes them false.

bp1000_3.plain: Saying 'it never rains here' is wrong the moment one wet day shows up in the record.
mem: NOT question: find the 3 true ones first.
'Always' and 'never' need zero exceptions.
The U-shape means the trend reverses.
bp1000_3.trap: Skimming the question and picking a true statement. Remember the question asks which is NOT supported.

ox: Correct. Table 1 gives 110% at 100 µM and 100% for the 0 µM vehicle control, so viability at 100 µM was higher.
Wrong. Table 1 gives 70% at 30 µM and 85% at 10 µM. 70 is lower than 85, so viability at 30 µM was lower, not higher.
Wrong. Table 1 gives 95% at 60 µM and 70% at 30 µM. 95 is higher than 70, so this is reversed.
Wrong. Viability did not fall steadily. It fell to 70% at 30 µM and then rose to 95% at 60 µM and 110% at 100 µM.

p: To check a comparison, find both rows and compare their numbers directly. Do not rely on memory of the overall trend.
A U-shaped (biphasic) response means the values go down and then come back up, so a statement about a steady trend is usually wrong.

bp1000_4.plain: Like comparing two test scores on a report card: look at both and see which number is bigger.
mem: Look up both rows, then compare.
The control is 100%; values above it mean more viable than baseline.
The minimum is at 30 µM (70%).
bp1000_4.trap: Assuming 'more compound means less viability' because the first drop looks steady. The table reverses at 60 and 100 µM.

ox: Correct. The table row for 50 uM lists Viability (%) = 60. The passage says results are a percentage of the untreated control, so 60 means cells kept 60% of control viability.
Wrong. 85% is the viability at 10 uM, not 50 uM. This is a row-reading mistake.
Wrong. 30% is the viability at 100 uM, the highest dose. It is the row below the one asked about.
Wrong. 100% is the 0 uM (untreated) value, the baseline the others are compared with.

p: A dose is how much drug the cells get. A response is what happens to the cells. Here, the response is viability: the percent of cells still alive compared with cells given no drug.
To read a table, find the row for the dose in the question, then move across to the right column. Always check the units in the column header.

bp1020_0.plain: It is like finding a train time on a schedule: pick the row for your station, then read the column for the time.
mem: Viability is given as a percent of the untreated control (0 uM = 100%).
Dose-dependent decrease means viability falls as concentration rises: 100, 85, 60, 30.
Match the question's dose to the right row before choosing.
bp1020_0.trap: Picking a neighboring row (85% or 30%) because the numbers look similar. Underline the dose in the question first.

ox: Wrong. Untreated cells get no solvent at all. They show baseline growth but cannot show whether the solvent alone harms cells.
Correct. Drug X must be dissolved in a solvent, so a vehicle-only group gets the solvent with no drug. Any difference between vehicle and drug-treated cells is then due to Drug X, not the solvent.
Wrong. A high-dose drug group still contains the drug, so it cannot isolate the effect of the solvent. It is a treatment group, not a control for the solvent.
Wrong. A low-dose drug group also contains the drug, so it cannot separate the solvent's effect from the drug's effect.

p: The vehicle is the liquid (such as a solvent) that carries a drug. Sometimes the vehicle itself affects cells. A vehicle control gets exactly the vehicle, with no drug.
Comparing drug cells with vehicle cells isolates the drug's effect. An untreated control is a different baseline: no drug and no vehicle.

bp1020_1.plain: If you test a medicine in juice, you also need a group that drinks only the juice.
mem: Vehicle control = solvent only, no drug.
Untreated control = no drug, no solvent.
Vary only one thing between the groups you compare.
bp1020_1.trap: Choosing 'untreated cells' because it sounds like the standard control. It does not account for the solvent.

ox: Correct. Percent decrease = (old - new) / old x 100. The table gives 85% at 10 uM and 30% at 100 uM, so (85 - 30) / 85 = 55/85, which is about 64.7%.
Wrong. 55 is the drop in percentage points (85 - 30), not the percent decrease. You must divide by the starting value, 85.
Wrong. 70 is the drop from 100 to 30 (the 0 uM to 100 uM change). The question starts at 10 uM, which is 85%.
Wrong. 85 is the viability at 10 uM, the starting value, not a decrease.

p: Percent decrease tells how big a drop is compared with where you started. Subtract the new value from the old, divide by the old, then multiply by 100.
Percentage points are different. Going from 85% to 30% is a drop of 55 percentage points, but a relative decrease of 55/85.

bp1020_2.plain: If a $85 shirt goes to $30, the discount is $55, and that $55 is a fraction of the original $85 price.
mem: Percent change = (change / starting value) x 100.
The starting value is the denominator.
Percentage points are not percent change.

fm.f: Percent decrease = (old - new) / old x 100, where old = viability at 10 uM and new = viability at 100 uM
fm.why: The question asks for the relative drop from 10 uM to 100 uM.
fm.nc: 55/85 = 11/17, a bit under 2/3 (0.667), so about 65%. Only 64.7% fits.

bp1020_2.sc: Estimate 55/85: it is a bit less than two thirds, so look for an answer near 65%.
bp1020_2.trap: Giving 55 (percentage points) or using 100 as the starting value instead of 85.

ox: Wrong. This is supported. Viability is 85% at 10 uM, 60% at 50 uM and 30% at 100 uM, all lower than 100% at 0 uM.
Wrong. This is supported. The table lists 100% viability at 0 uM, the untreated control.
Wrong. This is supported. Std Dev goes 2, 3, 4, 5 as concentration goes 0, 10, 50, 100 uM, matching the passage statement that standard deviations increased slightly.
Correct. The statement is NOT supported. The table gives viability at 100 uM as 30%, not 50%.

p: For 'NOT supported' questions, test each statement against the table. Three will match exactly. One will contain a wrong number or reversed trend.
Standard deviation (SD) measures how spread out replicate values are. A bigger SD means more variability.

bp1020_3.plain: It is like proofreading: compare each sentence with the source and find the one that does not match.
mem: Check each option against the table, one at a time.
Viability values: 100, 85, 60, 30.
SD values: 2, 3, 4, 5 (rising).
bp1020_3.trap: Assuming a plausible-sounding number like 50% is right. Verify against the 100 uM row.

ox: Correct. The passage reports a dose-dependent decrease in viability (down to 30% at 100 uM) and says the aim was to see whether Drug X could be a chemotherapeutic agent. That supports further study, not a final conclusion.
Wrong. Viability drops to 30% at 100 uM, so the drug is clearly toxic to cells at high doses. The passage also mentions 'minimizing toxicity' as a concern.
Wrong. Viability falls from 100% to 30%, so Drug X clearly has an effect.
Wrong. Viability fell, which means fewer living cells. The data give no sign of increased proliferation.

p: Cell-culture results are an early step. They show a drug can kill cancer cells in a dish. They do not prove safety or benefit in people.
So the best conclusion is modest: the drug is promising enough to study further.

bp1020_4.plain: A good test drive means you look at the car more seriously, not that you buy it on the spot.
mem: Lab-dish data support 'warrants further study'.
Lower viability means more cell killing.
Avoid options with absolute words like 'safe' or 'no effect'.
bp1020_4.trap: Choosing an overstated claim. Pick the conclusion that matches what the data can actually show.

ox: Wrong. 45 % is the viability at 40 µM in the table, not 20 µM.
Correct. In the table, the row for 20 µM shows viability of 70 (% of control).
Wrong. 85 % is the viability at 10 µM, one row above 20 µM.
Wrong. 20 % is the viability at 80 µM, the highest dose.

p: A dose is the amount of drug given. Viability is the percent of cells still alive compared with untreated cells. A dose-response table pairs each dose with its viability.
Find the dose row first, then read across to the value.

bp1100_0.plain: It is like finding a street on a map, then reading the house number next to it, not the one next door.
mem: Read across the matching row.
Viability falls as dose rises: 100, 85, 70, 45, 20.
Untreated control (0 µM) is 100%.
bp1100_0.trap: Reading the wrong row. The distractors are the neighboring and extreme values from the same column.

ox: Correct. The drug is dissolved in a solvent. A vehicle control gets the solvent alone, so any extra drop in viability with the drug is from the drug itself.
Wrong. A positive control uses a known toxic agent to show the assay can detect cell death. It does not show whether the solvent harms cells.
Wrong. A no-cell control measures background signal from the assay. It has no cells, so it says nothing about solvent toxicity.
Wrong. A time-zero measurement gives the starting viability. It does not separate drug effects from solvent effects over 48 hours.

p: A control is a comparison group that helps you interpret results. A vehicle control gets everything except the active drug: the same solvent at the same amount.
If the vehicle group looks like the untreated group, the solvent is harmless. Then any extra killing is due to the drug.

bp1100_1.plain: If you mix medicine into juice, you also test juice alone, to know whether the juice caused the upset stomach.
mem: Vehicle control = solvent alone.
Positive control proves the assay works.
Blank (no cells) corrects background signal.
bp1100_1.trap: Choosing the positive control because it sounds like it validates the experiment. It checks the assay, not the solvent.

ox: Wrong. 20 % is the remaining viability at 80 µM, not the decrease. The decrease is the part that was lost.
Wrong. 50 % does not match the control-to-80 µM change. It likely comes from subtracting 20 % from 70 % (the 20 µM value), which uses the wrong starting point.
Correct. The table gives 100 % for the control (0 µM) and 20 % at 80 µM. 100 - 20 = 80, so viability decreased by 80 %.
Wrong. A 100 % decrease would mean 0 % viability. The table shows 20 % remaining at 80 µM.

p: Percent decrease compares the final value with the starting value. Here the starting value is the control, 100 %.
Because the control is exactly 100, the decrease in percentage points equals the percent decrease.

bp1100_2.plain: If you had 100 coins and 20 are left, you lost 80 of them, which is 80%.
mem: Decrease = start - end.
Divide by the start. Here the start is 100.
Remaining and lost are not the same thing.

fm.f: Percent decrease = (control viability - treated viability) / control viability x 100, where control = viability with no drug and treated = viability at 80 µM
fm.why: The question compares the 80 µM result with the control.
fm.nc: With a base of 100, subtract and you are done: 100 - 20 = 80.

bp1100_2.trap: Giving the remaining viability (20 %) instead of the amount lost, or comparing the wrong two rows.

ox: Wrong. This statement is true. Viability falls from 100 to 85, 70, 45 and 20 as concentration rises.
Wrong. This statement is true. The SD values are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, which rise at each dose.
Correct. This is the FALSE statement. At 10 µM viability is 85 % and at 20 µM it is 70 %. So 10 µM has higher viability, not lower.
Wrong. This statement is true. The table lists 0 µM with viability 100, matching the passage's description of percent of untreated control.

p: Some questions ask which statement is FALSE. You must check every option and pick the one that the data contradict. The other three will be true.
Here, a higher dose should give lower viability. So a lower dose (10 µM) should have higher viability than 20 µM.

bp1100_3.plain: It is like a quiz where three people tell the truth and one lies. You hunt for the liar.
mem: Read the question word: FALSE or TRUE.
Check each option against the table.
In a dose-dependent kill, low dose means higher viability.
bp1100_3.trap: Switching to looking for a true statement. Option B uses the word 'increases', but SD really does rise, so it is true.

ox: Wrong. At 25 µM, viability on the straight line would be 70 - 5 x 1.25, about 64 %, still well above 50 %.
Wrong. At 30 µM the line gives about 70 - 10 x 1.25 = 57.5 %, still above 50 %.
Correct. Viability falls from 70 % at 20 µM to 45 % at 40 µM, a drop of 25 over 20 µM. To reach 50 % we need a drop of 20, which is 20/25 of the way: 0.8 x 20 = 16 µM past 20, so 36 µM.
Wrong. At 40 µM the table says viability is 45 %, which is already below 50 %.

p: Interpolation estimates a value between two known points. If we assume a straight line, we find what fraction of the total drop we need, then move the same fraction along the x-axis.
Here the target (50 %) lies between 70 % and 45 %.

bp1100_4.plain: If a ramp drops 25 steps over 20 feet, finding the spot where it has dropped 20 steps means going 4/5 of the way along.
mem: Fraction needed = needed change / total change.
Move that fraction along the x-axis interval.
Check that the answer lies between the two known points.

fm.f: Concentration = 20 + (70 - 50) / (70 - 45) x (40 - 20), where 70 and 45 are viabilities at 20 and 40 µM and 50 is the target viability
fm.why: A straight line between two points lets us find the in-between concentration.

bp1100_4.sc: The target 50 is closer to 45 than to 70, so the answer must be nearer 40 than 20. Only 36 fits well.
bp1100_4.trap: Picking 40 µM because 45 % is the nearest table value, without interpolating.

ox: Wrong. Control viability is 58%, the lowest in the table, because these cells got hydrogen peroxide with no protective compound.
Wrong. Treatment A (10 µM) has 71% viability. That is above control (58) but below Treatment B (84).

Correct. The table lists Cell Viability (%) as 58 for control, 71 for Treatment A, 84 for Treatment B and 78 for Treatment C. The largest value is 84, so Treatment B (Antiox-1 at 50 µM) is highest. The passage agrees: 'Antiox-1 at 50 µM produced the highest cell viability'.
Wrong. NAC (Treatment C) has 78% viability. That is the second highest, below Treatment B at 84%.

p: Cell viability is the percent of cells still alive at the end of the experiment. A higher number means more cells survived the stress.
To find the 'highest' group, scan the row for that one variable and pick the biggest number. Ignore the other rows, which measure different things.

bp1127_0.plain: It is like checking test scores in one column of a gradebook and picking the top score.
mem: Viability: higher = more living cells.
Apoptosis (programmed cell death) and ROS (reactive oxygen species, damaging reactive molecules) should be lower in a protective treatment.
Always read the row for the exact variable asked.
bp1127_0.sc: Scan only the row named in the question and compare the numbers directly.
bp1127_0.trap: Picking a group from the passage's general story instead of checking the exact row in the table.

ox: Wrong. Control has no compound at all, while Treatment A has Antiox-1 at 10 µM. This comparison tests compound versus no compound, not concentration.
Wrong. Control has no compound, and Treatment C is NAC, a different compound. Two things differ, so it isolates nothing about Antiox-1 concentration.
Correct. Treatment A is Antiox-1 at 10 µM and Treatment B is Antiox-1 at 50 µM. The compound is the same and only the dose changes, so any difference (viability 71 vs 84) reflects concentration.
Wrong. Treatment B is Antiox-1 at 50 µM and Treatment C is NAC at 20 µM. Both the compound and the dose differ, so you cannot tell which caused any change.

p: A fair comparison changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same. The thing you change is the independent variable.
Here the variable of interest is the dose of Antiox-1. So you need two groups that both get Antiox-1 but at different amounts.

bp1127_1.plain: To test if more sugar makes tea sweeter, you compare two cups of the same tea with different sugar amounts, not tea versus coffee.
mem: Same compound, different dose = tests dose.
Control vs treated = tests the compound itself.
If two things differ between groups, the result is confounded.
bp1127_1.trap: Choosing a pair that includes the control. That tests presence of the compound, not its concentration.

ox: Wrong. 40% would mean ROS fell from 150 to 90. That is the Treatment C value (90), not Treatment B (60).
Correct. Reduction = control - Treatment B = 150 - 60 = 90 µM. Percent reduction = 90 / 150 x 100 = 60%.
Wrong. 70% would need ROS to fall to 45 (30% of 150). The table gives 60, not 45.
Wrong. 80% would need ROS to fall to 30. The table gives 60 for Treatment B.

p: ROS means reactive oxygen species, molecules that damage cells. Percent reduction tells you what fraction of the starting amount was removed.
Always divide the drop by the starting (control) value, not by the new value.

bp1127_2.plain: If a $150 jacket goes on sale for $60, you saved $90, which is 60% of the original price.
mem: Percent change = (change / original) x 100.
Original is the baseline, here the control.
Simplify fractions: 90/150 = 3/5 = 60%.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (control ROS - treated ROS) / control ROS x 100, where control ROS is ROS in the untreated group and treated ROS is ROS in Treatment B
fm.why: It measures the drop as a share of the starting level.
fm.nc: Divide top and bottom by 30: 90/150 = 3/5, and 3/5 is 60%.

bp1127_2.trap: Dividing by 60 (the new value) instead of 150 (the baseline), or reporting the final value as a percent.

ox: Wrong. This is a correct reading. Treatment B has the best viability (84), lowest apoptosis (12) and lowest ROS (60) among the groups, matching the passage.
Wrong. This is a correct reading. Treatment A has 71% viability versus 78% for NAC, and ROS of 110 versus 90, so 10 µM is less effective.
Correct. The question asks for the incorrect statement. Control ROS is 150 µM, the HIGHEST value in the table, not the lowest. The lowest is Treatment B at 60.
Wrong. This is a correct reading. Treatment B has membrane potential 73%, above 45, 58 and 65.

p: When a question asks which statement is incorrect, three options are true and one is false. Check each against the table.
A control group is the untreated comparison. Here it received hydrogen peroxide but no protective compound, so it should show the most damage, meaning the highest ROS.

bp1127_3.plain: It is like checking a friend's claims against a scoreboard until one claim does not match.
mem: Control = worst damage in a protection experiment.
Lower ROS = better protection.
Read the question word 'incorrectly' twice.
bp1127_3.trap: Forgetting the question asks for the FALSE statement and choosing a true one.

ox: Correct. The passage says the work used 'cultured human fibroblasts' exposed to 200 µM hydrogen peroxide, and itself notes it 'warrant[s] further investigation in vivo'. Cells in a dish lack whole-body factors like absorption, metabolism and toxicity, so results may not apply to patients.
Wrong. A control group with no compound is required for good design. It is a strength, not a limitation.
Wrong. Including NAC, a known antioxidant, gives a benchmark. That is a strength.
Wrong. Measuring four outcomes gives a fuller picture. It does not stop the findings from being applied to patients.

p: In vitro means in a dish, using isolated cells. In vivo means in a living whole organism.
Cells in a dish skip many real-body steps, such as how a drug is absorbed, broken down, or affects other organs. So dish results need testing in animals or people.

bp1127_4.plain: A boat that floats in a bathtub may still sink in the ocean.
mem: In vitro = in glass or dish; in vivo = in a living body.
Cell-culture results are early evidence only.
Controls and comparators are strengths, not limitations.
bp1127_4.trap: Calling a good design feature, such as a control, a limitation.

ox: Wrong. At 5 µM proliferation is 85% of control, a reduction of only 15%.
Wrong. At 10 µM proliferation is 70% of control, a 30% reduction.
Wrong. At 20 µM proliferation is 45% of control, a 55% reduction. Higher doses go lower.
Correct. At 80 µM proliferation falls to 5% of control, the lowest value listed, so the reduction (95%) is the greatest.

p: Results are given as percent of the vehicle control (the untreated baseline, 100%). A lower number means less cell growth.
The greatest reduction is at the concentration with the smallest percent.

bp1148_0.plain: Like turning a dimmer switch down: the lowest brightness is the biggest drop from full light.
mem: Vehicle control = 100%.
Lowest % of control = greatest inhibition.
Dose-dependent = effect grows as dose grows.
bp1148_0.trap: Picking an early, moderate dose, or reading the wrong direction (the smallest number means the biggest drop).

ox: Wrong. Concentration was the variable the researchers changed (0, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80 µM), so it was not constant.
Correct. The passage says cells 'were seeded at a density of 1 × 10^5 cells per well' for every well, so seeding density was held constant.
Wrong. Proliferation relative to control was the outcome measured, and it varied from 100% down to 5%.
Wrong. Wells received either vehicle (0 µM) or drug, so this differed between wells.

p: The independent variable is what the researcher changes (drug dose). The dependent variable is what is measured (proliferation).
A controlled (constant) variable is kept the same for all groups, so it cannot explain the results.

bp1148_1.plain: In a plant-growth test, you give every plant the same pot and sunlight, and change only the fertilizer.
mem: Independent = changed on purpose.
Dependent = measured result.
Controlled = kept identical in all groups.
bp1148_1.trap: Calling the manipulated variable or the outcome 'constant'.

ox: Wrong. 45% is the proliferation that remains at 20 µM. The decrease is what was lost.
